1. Identification Strategy
- Primary: Difference-in-differences (DID) at the restaurant level, comparing changes in employment (FTEs from nonmanagement payroll hours) from pre- to post-policy in New Jersey (treated) versus eastern Pennsylvania (control).
- Complementary validation: 
  - Difference-in-discontinuities near the state border (restrict to restaurants close to the border on both sides) to tighten comparability.
  - Event-study at the county-month level using BLS-790/ES-202 eating-and-drinking-places employment (SIC 58), 1982–1996, to assess NJ–PA pre-trends and dynamic effects around April 1992.
- Rationale: The policy shock is plausibly exogenous with clear timing and geography. The restaurant-level panel (two waves) supports DID; the long ES-202 series enables credible pre-trend checks and dynamics at aggregate levels. The near-border design addresses spatial comparability and spillovers.

2. Treatment and Control
- Treatment variable: NJ × Post. Treated units are restaurants located in New Jersey. Post equals 1 for observations in Nov–Dec 1992; Pre equals 1 for Feb–Mar 1992.
- Control group: Restaurants from the same chains in eastern Pennsylvania zip-code areas that match the NJ coverage.
- Treatment timing / event date: Policy change on April 1, 1992; “Pre” observations are Feb–Mar 1992, “Post” observations are Nov–Dec 1992 (8–9 months after).
- Optional treatment intensity/heterogeneity: Indicator Bound_i = 1 if a restaurant’s pre-policy average nonmanagement wage was below $5.05 (i.e., likely binding). Where wage data are missing at the store level, proxy by chain×zip-area pre-policy average from the telephone-survey merge.

3. Key Identifying Assumptions
- Parallel trends (DID): Absent the NJ minimum-wage hike, NJ and eastern PA fast-food employment would have evolved similarly over the Pre→Post window.
  - Plausibility: States are adjacent, the sample is within similar zip-code areas and the same chains; the industry is highly comparable. Will be probed using ES-202 county-month data 1982–1991 and Jan–Mar 1992 to show similar pre-trends.
- No interference/spillovers across units: PA restaurants’ employment is not systematically affected by NJ’s policy via cross-border consumer shifts or labor flows.
  - Plausibility: Potential concern given geographic proximity. We will mitigate by (i) excluding PA units near the border, (ii) using very near-border DID (difference-in-discontinuities) to balance unobservables, and (iii) checking robustness to alternative PA samples.
- No differential contemporaneous shocks: No other policy or idiosyncratic shock differentially hit NJ fast food vs PA over the same window.
  - Plausibility: Reasonable for a short horizon, but we will adjust for chain fixed effects and local area fixed effects, and test with broader ES-202 series.
- Stable composition/measurement: The panel of restaurants is comparable across waves; employment measurement (hours converted to FTE) is consistent.
  - Plausibility: Administrative payroll data minimize measurement error; we will examine attrition/closures and conduct robustness with balanced panel and survival outcomes.

4. Threats to Identification and Mitigation
- Cross-border spillovers (product or labor market): NJ wage hike could shift demand or workers across the border, biasing the control.
  - Mitigation: 
    - Exclude PA stores within X miles (e.g., 10–20 miles) of the NJ border.
    - Run a border-focused DID (difference-in-discontinuities), restricting to symmetric near-border bands on both sides to improve comparability.
    - Check for price adjustments or hours mix changes (if available) that might imply competitive responses.
- Differential seasonality or local shocks between Feb–Mar and Nov–Dec by state:
  - Mitigation:
    - Include store fixed effects and a common Post indicator (two-way FE panel).
    - Validate parallel seasonal patterns in ES-202 data using monthly pre-trends in prior years, and by comparing NJ–PA differences in the same months of prior years (Nov–Dec vs Feb–Mar).
    - Add county unemployment controls in the ES-202 regressions; for store-level, include local area FE and chain FE.
- Sample selection/attrition (openings/closures):
  - Mitigation:
    - Estimate both on balanced panel and with an “intent-to-treat” approach that codes closures as zero FTE in Post (where defensible/available).
    - Model survival (LPM or logit) as an outcome in DID to test for differential exit.

5. R Code Outline

Assumptions:
- admin_fastfood_payroll.csv has: store_id, state (NJ/PA), zip_area, chain, pay_period_start, pay_period_end, nonmgmt_hours, avg_wage_nonmgmt (optional).
- telephone_survey.csv optional for pre-policy wage where payroll wage missing.
- es202_county_month.csv has: state, county_fips, year, month, emp_sic58.

R code:

# Packages
library(data.table)
library(fixest)
library(lubridate)
library(ggplot2)

# 1) Load administrative payroll data
adm <- fread("admin_fastfood_payroll.csv")

# Construct period indicator
adm[, start := as.Date(pay_period_start)]
adm[, end   := as.Date(pay_period_end)]
adm[, weeks := as.numeric(end - start + 1) / 7]

# Classify pre/post windows
adm[, period := fifelse(month(start) %in% c(2,3) & year(start)==1992, "pre",
                 fifelse(month(start) %in% c(11,12) & year(start)==1992, "post", NA_character_))]
adm <- adm[!is.na(period)]

# Average to store x period
adm[, weekly_hours := nonmgmt_hours / weeks]
panel <- adm[, .(
  weekly_hours = mean(weekly_hours, na.rm=TRUE),
  avg_wage_nonmgmt = if ("avg_wage_nonmgmt" %in% names(adm)) weighted.mean(avg_wage_nonmgmt, weeks, na.rm=TRUE) else NA_real_
), by=.(store_id, state, zip_area, chain, period)]

# Construct outcomes and DID covariates
panel[, fte := weekly_hours / 35]
panel <- panel[is.finite(fte) & fte > 0]  # drop nonpositive
panel[, lfte := log(fte)]
panel[, post := as.integer(period=="post")]
panel[, nj := as.integer(state=="NJ")]

# Optional: boundness using pre wage when available
pre_wage <- panel[period=="pre", .(store_id, avg_wage_nonmgmt_pre = avg_wage_nonmgmt)]
panel <- merge(panel, pre_wage, by="store_id", all.x=TRUE, suffixes=c("", "_prekeep"))
panel[, bound := as.integer(!is.na(avg_wage_nonmgmt_pre) & avg_wage_nonmgmt_pre < 5.05)]

# Main DID with store FE (preferred)
est_main <- feols(lfte ~ post + nj:post | store_id, data=panel, cluster=~zip_area)
summary(est_main)

# Alternative: levels outcome
est_levels <- feols(fte ~ post + nj:post | store_id, data=panel, cluster=~zip_area)
summary(est_levels)

# Robustness 1: Triple-difference focusing on bound stores (where bound defined)
# Include all lower-order terms explicitly
panel[, nj_post := nj*post]
panel[, bound_post := bound*post]
panel[, nj_bound_post := nj*bound*post]
est_ddd <- feols(lfte ~ post + nj_post + bound_post + nj_bound_post | store_id, data=panel, cluster=~zip_area)
summary(est_ddd)

# Robustness 2: Near-border difference-in-discontinuities
# Suppose we have distance to NJ border in km for each store (dist_to_nj_km; positive in PA, zero in NJ)
# If not available, approximate using zip centroid distances externally and merge before this step.
if ("dist_to_nj_km" %in% names(panel)) {
  nearband <- panel[ (state=="NJ" & dist_to_nj_km <= 20) | (state=="PA" & dist_to_nj_km <= 20) ]
  est_border <- feols(lfte ~ post + nj:post | store_id, data=nearband, cluster=~zip_area)
  summary(est_border)
}

# Weighting sensitivity: weight by baseline size (pre FTE)
pre_size <- panel[period=="pre", .(store_id, fte_pre = fte)]
panel <- merge(panel, pre_size, by="store_id", all.x=TRUE)
est_wt <- feols(lfte ~ post + nj:post | store_id, data=panel, weights=~fte_pre, cluster=~zip_area)
summary(est_wt)

# 2) Event study using ES-202 county-month (SIC 58) to check pre-trends/dynamics
es <- fread("es202_county_month.csv")
# Keep NJ and PA
es <- es[state %in% c("NJ","PA")]
es[, ym := make_date(year, month, 1L)]
es[, treat := as.integer(state=="NJ")]
# Event time relative to April 1992
es[, et := (year*12 + month) - (1992*12 + 4)]
# Outcome
es[, lemp := log(emp_sic58)]
# TWFE event study with county and month-year FE
# Create factor for ym for FE
est_es <- feols(lemp ~ i(et, treat, ref=-1, drop=c(-100:-25, 25:100)) | county_fips + ym, data=es, cluster=~county_fips)
summary(est_es)

# Plot event coefficients
event_df <- broom::tidy(est_es)[grepl("fit::et::", term)]
ggplot(event_df, aes(x = as.numeric(gsub("\\D", "", term)), y = estimate)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept=0, linetype="dashed") +
  geom_point() + geom_errorbar(aes(ymin=estimate-1.96*std.error, ymax=estimate+1.96*std.error)) +
  xlab("Months relative to Apr 1992") + ylab("Log employment: NJ vs PA (baseline = t=-1)")

6. Expected Results
- Competitive short-run labor demand implies a negative effect on employment among bound restaurants. A commonly cited short-run own-wage elasticity of labor demand in low-wage services is roughly −0.1 to −0.3. With an 18.8% wage increase, this implies:
  - Bound restaurants: employment change ≈ −1.9% to −5.6%.
  - Overall average across all restaurants (including unbound): attenuated toward zero depending on the share bound.
- Net expectation: small negative effect in the full sample; more negative among bound units.

7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DID)
- C1: Parallel trends between NJ and eastern PA in fast-food employment pre-1992 (validated with ES-202 pre-trends) — 1
- C2: No anticipation/clean timing (policy effective Apr 1, 1992; pre data Feb–Mar 1992) — 1
- C3: Stable sample/measurement and no differential attrition (tested via balanced panel and survival outcome) — 1
- C4: No spillovers/interference across states — 0 (plausible concern; addressed via buffers/border design but not guaranteed)
- C5: No other contemporaneous shocks differentially affecting NJ fast food — 1

Notes on interpretation
- Preferred coefficient: nj:post in the store-FE regression on log FTE. This estimates the average treatment effect on treated restaurants in NJ relative to PA. The DDD coefficient nj_bound_post isolates the effect on restaurants likely bound by the new minimum wage.
